nameStory: Micrasterias gets its name from Greek words meaning 'small star,' referring to the beautiful star-like shape of these microscopic algae. The species name 'foliacea' means 'leafy,' describing how this tiny organism looks like an intricate, ornate leaf when viewed under magnification.
description: Micrasterias foliacea is a single-celled freshwater alga that's invisible to the naked eye, measuring only about 0.1-0.2 millimeters across. Under a microscope, it reveals itself as one of nature's most beautiful geometric designs - a symmetrical, star-shaped cell with elaborate lobes and intricate patterns that look like tiny snowflakes or ornate leaves. These algae live in clean, acidic ponds and bogs throughout New England. You'll need a microscope to see these amazing creatures, but they're worth the effort for their stunning beauty.

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: The cell is perfectly symmetrical with a distinctive constriction in the middle, creating two mirror-image halves that look like elaborate stars or snowflakes

idTips.label: Lobed margins
idTips.description: The outer edges have multiple deep lobes with pointed tips, creating an ornate, leaf-like appearance with intricate indentations

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: The cell appears bright green under the microscope due to chloroplasts (the parts that capture sunlight for photosynthesis)

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Measures roughly 100-200 micrometers across - about twice the width of a human hair, requiring at least 100x magnification to see details

idTips.label: Rigid cell wall
idTips.description: The cell maintains its precise shape due to a firm outer wall, unlike soft algae that change shape when they move

habitat: Found in clean, soft-water ponds, bog pools, and quiet backwaters of streams throughout New England's forests and wetlands. Prefers acidic water with low mineral content, often in areas with sphagnum moss and other acid-loving plants. Most common in undisturbed wilderness areas away from agricultural runoff or development.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms and daylight increases. Best viewing in late spring when numbers peak before summer heat.
seasonality.summer: Present but may be less abundant during hot weather. Early morning or evening collection from shaded water gives best results.
seasonality.fall: Often shows a second population boom as temperatures cool. Excellent time for observation as water clarity improves.
seasonality.winter: Dormant or present in very low numbers under ice. Not typically observed during winter months in New England.

funFact: Each Micrasterias cell is essentially a living piece of art - the intricate patterns are so precise and beautiful that Victorian-era microscopists used them as artistic inspiration for wallpaper and textile designs, calling them 'the jewels of the pond.'
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other star-shaped desmid algae like Micrasterias truncata or Micrasterias rotata. Look for the specific lobe patterns - foliacea has more deeply divided, leaf-like lobes compared to the broader, simpler lobes of its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being single-celled, these algae are not bacteria - they're actually more closely related to land plants and have complex internal structures including a nucleus. The beautiful patterns aren't just decoration; they help maximize surface area for absorbing nutrients from the water.
compareHints: Micrasterias foliacea has more deeply divided, ornate lobes compared to M. truncata which has broader, less intricate margins. Unlike M. rotata which appears more circular, foliacea has a distinctly leaf-like appearance with sharper points. The 'leafy' quality of its lobes makes it one of the most ornate species in the genus.
